title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarking, Runbooks, and Known Issues
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
=======
This document consolidates the serving runtime guidance maintained by the Serving Runtime team: architecture overview, kernel and scheduling model, profiling and performance playbooks, benchmarking suite instructions, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers onboarding on runtime work, SREs troubleshooting latency/regression issues, and product/QA teams validating performance SLAs.

Goals and scope
----------------
- Describe the runtime architecture and how components interact at request time.
- Define kernel selection and scheduling heuristics used for inference optimization.
- Provide a repeatable profiling/playbook for diagnosing latency and throughput regressions.
- Document the internal benchmarking harness and how to add new models/fixtures.
- Surface active known issues and mitigation/workarounds.
- Include runbooks for common operational scenarios (OOM, degraded throughput, tail latency).

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Runtime product owner: Maya Chen (author)
- Team: Serving Runtime (eng)
- Oncall rotation: serving-runtime@redwood-internal (Slack channel #serving-runtime)
- Pager owner: Diego Ramos

Architecture overview (short)
----------------------------
At a high level the serving runtime implements:
1) Front proxy layer (ingress) - handles authentication, per-tenant routing, and request validation.
2) Router & autoscaler - routes requests to GPU pools or CPU fallback nodes based on policy (latency, cost, region).
3) Execution shards - each shard runs an instance of the inference engine (C++ runtime) with:
   - Model loader and KV-cache manager
   - Scheduler (micro-batching and cooperative multitasking)
   - Kernel selection layer (operator fusion, quantization-aware kernels)
4) Observability hooks - token-level tracing, per-request span, and metrics (latency P50/P95/P99, GPU util, mem usage).

Sequence at request-time
1. Ingress receives request and validates auth/token.
2. Router resolves model variant and preferred pool using policy table.
3. Request is placed onto the shard queue for batching.
4. Scheduler groups the request into a micro-batch and selects kernels based on model profile & sequence length.
5. Inference executed, KV cache consulted/updated for chat sessions.
6. Response streamed back via ingress with trace id and cost accounting.

Key runtime components and responsibilities
- Model Catalog Adapter: ensures model artifacts and quantization profiles are compatible with runtime.
- Kernel Selector: chooses optimized kernels per operator based on sequence lengths and hardware.
- Scheduler: implements continuous batching, deadline-aware prioritization, and preemption for high-priority requests.
- KV Cache: per-session prefix caching to avoid re-computing common prefixes.
- Fallback Manager: routes to cheaper model variant or CPU fallback when GPU capacity is constrained.

Kernel selection and scheduling (detailed)
----------------------------------------
Design goals:
- Prioritize latency SLO adherence for latency-critical routes.
- Maximize utilization while avoiding tail-latency amplification.
- Use quantization-friendly kernels where quality regression is acceptable.

Heuristics used by Kernel Selector:
- Model architecture fingerprint (decoder-only, encoder-decoder) -> baseline kernel set.
- Sequence length histogram (recent 1h window) -> choose long-sequence kernels when >30% sequences >512 tokens.
- Quantization profile: if model variant is q4/q8-compatible, prefer quant kernels and int OPs for matmuls.
- Hardware capabilities: CUDA compute capability and tensor core availability -> enable fused kernels.

Scheduler primitives and policies:
- Continuous batching: requests are placed into a run loop and batched for up to batch_max_latency_ms (default 8ms) or until batch_size target reached.
- Deadline-aware priority: requests carry a deadline SLO and are prioritized higher if close to expiry.
- Cooperative preemption: long-running lower-priority batches can be preempted to serve high-priority low-latency requests; partial progress is cached to resume.
- Backpressure signals: when GPU queue depth > queue_high_threshold (default 256), router returns a 429 or routes to fallback pool depending on route policy.

Config knobs (examples)
- batch_max_latency_ms: 8
- batch_max_tokens: 4096
- queue_high_threshold: 256
- preemption_enabled: true
- short_seq_kernel_threshold: 128

Profiling and diagnosis playbook
--------------------------------
This playbook is used for investigating performance regressions (latency P95/P99 spikes, throughput drops, increased error rates). Follow steps in order:
1) Verify symptom and scope
   - Check SLO dashboards (per-route P50/P95/P99) and allocate time window.
   - Isolate to tenant/route/model/version or global? Use trace id examples.
2) Gather traces and metrics
   - Request-level spans (ingress->router->shard->kernel) for impacted traces.
   - GPU-level metrics: util, SM occupancy, GPU mem alloc, memcpy times.
   - Host-level: dmesg, oom-killer logs, scheduler latency histograms.
   - Collector commands:
     - rtrace fetch --trace-id=<trace>
     - nvtop or nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
3) Reproduce in perf lab (if safe)
   - Use the benchmarking harness (see Benchmarking Suite) and the same model/version/sequence length distribution.
   - Run with ENABLE_KV_CACHE=0/1 to test cache impact.
4) Narrow down layer: ingress/router/scheduler/kernel/driver
   - If scheduler wait time high -> adjust batch_max_latency_ms or check preemption settings.
   - If kernel compute high but GPU util low -> check memory-bound operations, avoid host-device copies, or switch kernel variant.
   - If memcpy time or PCIe saturation high -> check host NIC/PCIe troubleshooting.
5) Temporary mitigations
   - Route to a warm dedicated pool with higher concurrency.
   - Increase batch_max_latency_ms temporarily to raise throughput.
   - Roll back kernel flag or model variant causing regression.
6) Root cause and fix
   - Submit an ADR or code change with benchmarking evidence.
   - Schedule rollout with canary and monitoring (see Rollout checklist below).

Benchmarking suite (how to run and extend)
-----------------------------------------
Purpose: produce reproducible latency and throughput baselines for model variants across hardware profiles. Bench harness is located in repo infra/benchmarks/serving-harness.

Quickstart (perf lab)
1. Checkout: git clone internal:infra/benchmarks; cd serving-harness
2. Prepare model artifacts: use model-registry CLI to pin model version: model-registry get --model llama-13b --version v2 --output ./artifacts
3. Launch benchmark job (example):
   ./run_benchmark.sh --artifacts ./artifacts --profile a100-80gb --seq-dist short=70,long=30 --qos latency --target-qps 100 --duration 600
4. Artifacts produced: latency.csv, gpu_metrics.csv, scheduler_metrics.json, kernel_choices.log

Extending the harness:
- Add a new model fixture by creating a JSON descriptor under fixtures/models/ with keys: model_name, architecture, tokenizer, expected_peak_mem, recommended_kernels (list).
- Add hardware profile under fixtures/hardware/ with GPU type, PCIe bandwidth, NUMA layout.
- Tests must include a golden baseline assertion file in fixtures/goldens/. CI will run benchmarks for PRs that touch runtime code.

Benchmarking best-practices
- Use a cold/warm run strategy: 3 cold iterations, 5 warm iterations, then 10 measured iterations.
- Ensure model shard placement is pinned for repeatability (use --pin-shards).
- Capture system noise by running an empty-run baseline and subtracting overhead.

Runtime runbooks (operational)
----------------------------
Runbook: High tail latency (P99 spike)
1. Confirm alert: Check alert channel #alerts-serving-runtime.
2. Gather affected routes and trace ids.
3. Run rtrace aggregate --window 15m and inspect scheduler wait times.
4. If queue depth high:
   - Temporarily increase batch_max_latency_ms by 5ms for impacted pool.
   - If that does not remediate, route to pre-warmed dedicated pool.
5. If kernel hot-path shows large compute time increase: rollback kernel flag via feature-flag system.
6. Post-incident: run benchmark for that model and attach artifacts to postmortem.

Runbook: GPU OOM during model load
1. Evict non-critical models from the pool: curl -X POST $CONTROL_PLANE/pools/{pool}/evict?model=noncritical
2. Restart model-loader on shard after clearing model cache: systemctl restart runtime-model-loader
3. If continuing OOMs: scale up node pool or bump node memory/GPU profile.

Runbook: Degraded throughput (throughput drop > 30%)
1. Check router logs for 429s and fallback routing.
2. Run ./inspect_queue.sh --pool <pool> to measure average batch sizes and latency.
3. If many tiny batches occur: increase batch_max_latency_ms by 3ms and monitor.
4. If small batches persist, check incoming request distribution and advise product to increase concurrency per route.

Known issues (active)
--------------------
- K-2026-01: Tensor core fused matmul at very small batch sizes can be slower than baseline on A100 L2 driver 525.x. Workaround: force non-fused kernel for batch_size < 8. Status: in_progress (driver team coordination).
- K-2026-02: Intermittent tail GC spikes on model-loader when model artifacts hit >60k files in a single bucket. Workaround: shard model artifacts across buckets and enable lazy-load. Status: mitigated (documented).
- K-2025-11: KV cache evictions not consistent across restarts leading to transient latency for chat sessions. Workaround: warm KV cache during node startup using warmup tool. Status: fixed in v1.12.3 but watch for regressions.

Release notes highlights (recent)
-------------------------------
v1.12.3 (2026-01-28)
- Fix: KV cache persistence bug causing cache thrash on restart.
- Perf: default batch_max_latency_ms reduced from 10ms to 8ms improving median latency by 12% for short-sequence workloads.
- Known issue: K-2026-01 identified with fused kernels.

v1.13.0-alpha (2026-02-10)
- Feature: deadline-aware preemption enabled behind feature flag.
- Feature: kernel selector now uses rolling 1h sequence-length histogram.
- Perf test: initial A/B shows 5% throughput improvement on long sequence workloads.

Rollout checklist
- Cut feature flag and enable on canary pool (5% traffic) for 24h, monitor P50/P95/P99 and error budget burn.
- If metrics stable, expand to 25% for 12h, then to 100% over 48h.
- Prepare rollback plan with explicit flag to disable.

Appendices
---------
A. Example kernel-choice log snippet:
[2026-02-10T14:17:02Z] model=llama-13b seq=64 chosen_kernel=fused_matmul_v2 quant=none gpu=a100-80gb
[2026-02-10T14:17:06Z] model=llama-13b seq=1024 chosen_kernel=longseq_block_matmul quant=q4 gpu=a100-80gb

B. Useful commands and queries
- rtrace fetch --trace-id=<trace-id> --output=json
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o DT --delay=1
- ./run_benchmark.sh --profile a100-80gb --seq-dist short=100

Caveats and future work
- We plan to add NUMA-aware placement heuristics to reduce host-device memcpy times.
- Ongoing work with driver and hardware teams to resolve K-2026-01 and enable safe fused kernels across batch sizes.
